generation.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Electric Power Monthly (Form EIA-923), net generation by state and source, grouped by the ERW (docs/methods/generation_mix.md)
generation.hourly_reason: No public source gives a state's generation by the hour; the hourly picture is by balancing authority, in the Grid tool.

retail.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-861M, retail sales and average price by state and sector
retail.revenue_note: Revenue is EIA's sales times EIA's average price for the same month and sector. EIA computes its average price as revenue over sales, so the product gives EIA's revenue to within the price's rounding (one tenth of a dollar a MWh).

plants.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Preliminary Monthly Electric Generator Inventory (Form EIA-860M)
plants.unit: MW (nameplate and net summer); MWh (storage energy)
plants.retired_note: EIA-860M's retired sheet as the ERW's table holds it: the generators retired in its window, not every retirement since 2001.

co2.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, State Electricity Profiles, emissions by state by fuel
co2.unit: metric tons of CO2; kg of CO2 per MWh

gas.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Natural Gas Monthly, consumption by end use and production by state

energy.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, State Energy Data System

by_sector_reason.commercial: the warehouse's SEDS tables hold the commercial sector's electricity and natural gas, not its total energy
by_sector_reason.transportation: the warehouse's SEDS tables hold the transportation sector's electricity and natural gas, not its total energy

disposition.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, State Electricity Profiles, source and disposition
disposition.note: Net interstate trade is EIA's figure, a line of the disposition: positive where the state sent more electricity to other states than it took in from them, below zero where it took in more.

serving.source: U.S. Census Bureau county population estimates, and Form EIA-861's utilities and balancing authorities by county, as the ERW's table eia_county_region joins them

by_authority.name: Western Area Power Administration - Rocky Mountain Region

by_authority.reason: its utilities name no balancing authority in EIA-861's sales file

serving.basis: Each county counts once, whole, for its primary authority: the one whose utilities serve most of the county's customers in EIA-861. A county two authorities share is counted for its primary one.

large_load_laws.source: The ERW's large-load research files, each law read at its legislature's or regulator's own page

laws.title: Large Load Customer Regulation Act (A BILL FOR AN ACT relating to electricity)
laws.threshold: a retail load customer requesting a new or expanded interconnection where the total load at a single site would exceed 20 MW
laws.requirements: interconnection study: public power suppliers must set interconnection standards including a study fee of 50,000 dollars or 1,000 dollars per MW, whichever is greater, with the study completed within one year of receiving the fee, and an additional fee for added capacity [p. 1, Sec. 3(1)(c): "(c) A study fee of fifty thousand dollars or one thousand dollars per megawatt, whichever is greater, to be paid to the interconnecting public power supplier for initial studies" | p. 1, Sec. 3(1)(c): "The public power supplier shall complete the study within one year after receiving the study fee;"] || disclosure: each large load customer must disclose any substantially similar request for service elsewhere that would make it change, delay or withdraw the request, and its onsite backup generating facilities [p. 1, Sec. 3(1)(a): "(a) A requirement for each large load customer to disclose to the interconnecting public power supplier whether the customer is pursuing a substantially similar request for electric service" | p. 1, Sec. 3(1)(b): "(b) A requirement for each interconnected large load customer to disclose to the interconnecting public power supplier information about the customer's onsite backup generating facilities."] || collateral: the standards must include a way to demonstrate site control and financial commitment requirements for the transmission and generation needed to serve the customer [p. 1, Sec. 3(1)(d): "(d) A method for a large load customer to demonstrate site control for the proposed load location; and" | p. 1, Sec. 3(1)(e): "(e) Financial commitment requirements for the development of transmission and generation infrastructure needed to serve a large load customer."] || cost allocation: a public power supplier may set or negotiate rates, charges and operating standards for each large load customer that fairly allocate system costs to it and mitigate operational, resource adequacy and financial risks to other customers [p. 1, Sec. 3(2): "(2) A public power supplier is authorized to establish or negotiate rates, charges, and operating standards for each large load customer that fairly allocate electricity system costs to the large load customer"] || curtailment or backup generation: public power suppliers must develop a procedure to procure demand response and load flexibility from large load customers and, in grid instability or emergencies, require them to curtail load or run onsite backup generation [p. 1, Sec. 4: "Sec. 4. Public power suppliers shall develop a procedure to: (1) Procure demand response, reductions, and load flexibility from large" | p. 2, Sec. 4(2): "the affected large load customers to curtail load or, for those customers with onsite backup generating facilities, to deploy such facilities"]

severance.reason: the severance tool holds Texas, Louisiana, New Mexico only
